paragraphs.source_en: The dominance of Shi‘ism and the Shi‘a ulema was also accompanied by a period of creativity in Shi‘a thought—notably among the thinkers who have been called the School of Isfahan (Mir Damad, Mir Fendereski, and Shaykh Baha’i), and the religious philosophy of the great Molla Sadra. Molla Sadra was born in Shiraz in 1571 or 1572. He studied in Qazvin and Isfahan as a young man, being interested in philosophy and the usual religious studies as well as Sufism. He was taught by two great thinkers of the age, Mir Damad and Shaykh Baha’i, and spent some time living near Qom and traveling before finally settling as a teacher in Shiraz again. His ideas (most notably expressed in the book known as al-Afsar al-arba’a—Four Journeys) drew upon the philosophy of Avicenna and Neoplatonism, but also on traditional Shi‘a thought and on the Sufism of Sohravardi (Illuminationism), and Ibn Arabi.
